q: Fodor argues his a priori conditions on propositional attitudes (PAs) demand treating them as:
w: Dispositions to behave in certain ways
Relations to natural-language sentences
Brain states with no internal structure
e: Relations between organisms and internal representations. This converges with what cognitive psychologists arrived at independently, which he takes as a reason to think it's true.

q: Condition I says PAs should be analyzed as relations. What's the only known alternative, which Fodor calls hopeless?
w: The operator view
Functionalism
Eliminativism
e: The 'fusion' view: 'believes-it's-raining' is a single unstructured predicate. On fusion, 'John believes it's raining' is atomic, like 'John is purple'. 'Talk about counter-intuitive!'

q: Which is one of Fodor's objections to the fusion view?
a: Infinitely many atomic predicates would be unlearnable
w: It wrongly makes belief a relation to something
It explains the opacity of belief contexts too well
It requires us to posit internal representations
e: There are infinitely many 'a believes ___' sentences, so if each were atomic, how could English be learned?. Davidson's learnability point. Also: on fusion, it's an accident that 'it will rain' appears in both 'fears' and 'believes' sentences.

q: 'Vendler's Condition' requires a theory of PAs to explain:
a: The parallel between attitude verbs and saying verbs
w: The opacity of belief contexts to substitution
The logical form of the objects of belief
How animals without language can have beliefs
e: The parallelism between verbs of propositional attitude and verbs of saying. What we can believe/hope/doubt are the very things we can assert/inquire/demand.

q: 'Frege's Condition' requires a theory of PAs to account for their:
w: Logical form
Causal powers
Parallel with verbs of saying
e: Opacity: substitution of identicals and existential generalization can fail inside belief contexts. Fodor notes fusion does satisfy this one, which shows Frege's condition alone under-constrains a theory.

q: 'Aristotle's Condition' says the objects of PAs have logical form. The paradigm example is:
w: Descartes' Cogito
Searle's Chinese Room
A modus tollens argument
e: The practical syllogism (John believes washing his car will make it rain, wants rain, so washes his car). Mental states interact causally in virtue of their content, and the generalizations refer to their form.

q: Answering 'if John believes P & Q, P & Q is inferentially inert', Fodor distinguishes:
a: What's entailed by the belief vs. by believing it
w: The syntax of a belief vs. its semantic content
Belief types vs. the individual belief tokens
Analytic beliefs vs. synthetic beliefs about facts
e: What's entailed by what's believed vs. what's entailed by believing it. P & Q always entails P. It's 'John believes P & Q' that isn't subject to simplification of conjunction.

q: Condition V requires a theory of PAs to:
a: Fit with empirical accounts of mental processes
w: Be provable entirely a priori, without experiment
Reduce completely and directly to physics
Avoid all reference to the brain and its parts
e: Mesh with empirical accounts of mental processes (e.g., 'cost accounting' of complexity). Analogy: 'water is H2O' must, with empirical premises, explain water's properties.

q: Carnap's theory construes PAs as relations between people and:
w: Abstract, language-independent propositions
The states of their brains at the time
Formulae in an innate internal code
e: Natural-language sentences they're disposed to utter. It handles conditions I–V surprisingly well, but runs into objections 1–7.

q: Brown and Lenneberg's 'codability' experiments found that:
a: Easily described colors were easier to remember
w: Color categories are entirely innate and fixed
Language plays no role at all in color memory
Dani speakers cannot perceive color differences
e: Colors with simpler English descriptions were easier to recognize and recall. This fits Carnap: what you (opaquely) remember is the description.

q: Which is the easiest objection to Carnap to fix, per Fodor?
w: That dogs have beliefs without language
That first languages must be learned
That some beliefs may be inexpressible
e: His account of the belief relation is behavioristic (dispositions to utter). The fix is to turn functionalist: a token of 'it's raining' plays a certain causal role.

q: The Dani findings are 'a shock' for Carnap's theory because:
a: English codability predicted Dani speakers' recall
w: Dani speakers had perfect memory for every color
Dani speakers couldn't recall any colors at all
The Dani language turned out to be like English
e: English codability predicted recall for Dani speakers, whose language has no chromatic color vocabulary. How could English sentences be objects of a monolingual Dani's attitudes?

q: Objection 7 against Carnap is circularity about:
w: The opacity of belief contexts
The logical form of beliefs
The parallel with verbs of saying
e: First-language learning, which itself requires beliefs, hypotheses and expectations. So some PAs must not be relations to natural-language sentences.

q: Fodor's solution keeps which part of Carnap's theory and drops which part?
w: Keeps behaviorism, drops sentences
Keeps natural language, drops sentences
Keeps dispositions, drops relations
e: Keeps: objects of PAs are sentences. Drops: they're NATURAL-language sentences. Objects of PAs are formulae in an Internal Representational System, a language of thought.

q: Fodor assumes the internal representational system is:
w: Learned from English
Unique to each person
Identical to Mandarin
e: Innate and universal (to the extent an organism shares our mental processes). That would explain the Dani data and language learning. If Whorf-Sapir turned out true, the theory could fail.

q: What does Fodor's 'they are flying planes' example show?
a: Speakers must internally represent a grammar
w: English sentences are never truly ambiguous
Grammars are abstract Platonic objects only
Sentences have no internal structure at all
e: Psycholinguistics needs a grammar that speakers internally represent, so internal representations are required anyway. Why the grammar and not some 'schmamar'? Only because G-proper is the system speakers actually use to represent sentences.

q: Why won't Fodor just say 'PAs are relations to propositions. Punkt!'?
a: Propositions lack form needed for computation
w: Propositions simply don't exist at all
Propositions are just states of the brain
Frege proved such a view is impossible
e: Propositions lack form (bad for computation), and he can't see how organisms relate to them except via internal formulae. Propositions can be MEDIATE objects of PAs, with internal representations doing the mediating.

q: Fodor says if the representational theory of mind is true, the main remaining problem for philosophy of mind is:
a: How internal representations relate to the world
w: Whether brains really exist outside of our minds
How we should define the ordinary word 'belief'
Whether animals have minds like our own
e: What relates internal representations to the world (their semantic interpretation). 'Psychology is all the philosophy of mind that we are likely to get.'
